# lslearn

lslearn implements **Coordinated Multi-Neighborhood Learning (CML)**, a
constraint-based algorithm for learning the *local* causal structure
around a set of user-specified target nodes in a directed acyclic graph
(DAG), without estimating the entire graph structure or the subset of
the graph that is not directly relevant to the target nodes.

## Why local structure learning?

Global causal discovery algorithms (e.g. PC, FCI) attempt to recover
information encoded in the whole DAG, but this is often more than
researchers need and scales poorly as the number of variables grows. In
many applications, the research question only requires recovering the
parents (and children) of a small set of target nodes, so that their
causal effects can be estimated via the back-door adjustment. For
example, this approach could be used to identify the regulators of a set
of selected genes in a gene regulatory network.

lslearn’s algorithms restrict computation to the neighborhoods of the
target nodes:

- **CML** estimates the local structure around *multiple* target
  neighborhoods simultaneously, coordinating edge orientation between
  them. Even when target neighborhoods are disjoint, causal information
  can propagate between them through ancestral relationships (inducing
  paths), which lets CML orient edges that would be unidentifiable if
  each neighborhood were learned in isolation.
- **SNL** (Single Neighborhood Learning) is the uncoordinated baseline:
  it applies constraint-based structure learning to each target
  neighborhood independently without recourse to any rules to translate
  ancestral information between neighborhoods.

Both algorithms first estimate the first- and second-order neighbors of
each target node, then recover the local skeleton via conditional
independence (CI) testing. The rules for edge orientation is where both
algorithms diverge. The CML algorithm orients edges using a subset of
FCI’s rules and a specialized rule for the local learning context. The
SNL algorithm uses Meek’s (from the PC algorithm) for basic edge
orientation.

Compared to applying a global algorithm and restricting attention to the
target neighborhoods afterward, CML is both more accurate by avoiding
errors from other parts of the graph and cheaper computationally, since
the number of conditional independence tests scales with the size of the
target neighborhoods rather than the size of the whole network.

### Reference

Smith, S. and Zhou, Q. (2026). *Coordinated Multi-Neighborhood Learning
on a Directed Acyclic Graph.*

The paper includes the algorithm details, soundness/completeness
results, consistency guarantees (including in the high-dimensional
setting), and empirical comparisons against the global PC algorithm and
the SNL baseline on both simulated networks and a gene expression data
set.

## Status

lslearn is a ground-up, more rigorously engineered reimplementation of
the algorithms originally prototyped in
[stephenvsmith/CML](https://github.com/stephenvsmith/CML), the package
used to produce the results in the paper above. The migration is in
progress and being landed in small, reviewable pieces, so not all
algorithms described in the paper are implemented and exported yet.
Check the [issues](https://github.com/stephenvsmith/lslearn/issues) and
open pull requests for the current state of the migration.

## Installation

lslearn is not yet on CRAN. Install the development version from
[GitHub](https://github.com/stephenvsmith/lslearn) with:

``` r

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("stephenvsmith/lslearn")
```

Because lslearn links to compiled code (via Rcpp and RcppArmadillo) and
imports packages with their own system requirements, installing it
requires:

- A C++ compiler toolchain (Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, Rtools on
  Windows, or build-essential on Debian/Ubuntu).
- The [GNU Scientific Library](https://www.gnu.org/software/gsl/) (GSL),
  required by one of lslearn’s dependencies. Install it via
  `brew install gsl` on macOS or `apt install libgsl-dev` on
  Debian/Ubuntu before installing lslearn.

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. This section covers how to get a local
development environment set up.

### Prerequisites

- A recent R release (4.4 or later is recommended — some dependencies
  may not have binaries available for older R versions on all
  platforms).
- [GSL](https://www.gnu.org/software/gsl/) and a C++ toolchain, as
  described above.
- [Pandoc](https://pandoc.org/), needed to build package documentation
  and the pkgdown site.
- [`pre-commit`](https://pre-commit.com/#install), the tool that runs
  this repo’s code quality checks. Install it with
  `pipx install pre-commit`, `brew install pre-commit`, or
  `pip install pre-commit`.

### Setup

1.  Clone the repository and open it in R (or RStudio) at the repo root,
    so that `.Rprofile` activates the project’s
    [renv](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) environment automatically.

2.  Install the git hooks defined in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:

    ``` sh
    pre-commit install
    ```

    This setup includes three stages:

    - **pre-commit**: automatically styles and lints changed R files
      (`styler`, `lintr`), regenerates `NAMESPACE`/documentation when
      needed, formats changed C++ files (`clang-format`), and
      regenerates `RcppExports` when files under `src/` change.
    - **commit-msg**: enforces a [Conventional
      Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) style commit
      message (via `commitizen`), e.g. `fix: ...`, `feat: ...`,
      `build: ...`.
    - **pre-push**: runs a full `R CMD check` before code is pushed.

3.  Install lslearn’s dependencies and build the package itself:

    ``` r

    renv::install(".")
    ```

    This resolves and installs whatever dependency versions currently
    satisfy `DESCRIPTION`, then builds and installs lslearn. If you
    instead want the exact dependency versions pinned in `renv.lock`
    (what CI uses), run
    [`renv::restore()`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/reference/restore.html)
    first — note this can occasionally be slower if a pinned version
    predates the binaries CRAN currently serves for your R version.

### Running tests

``` r

testthat::test_check("lslearn")
```

or run the full package check that mirrors CI:

``` r

rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(".", args = "--no-manual")
```

(Run these from an R console, e.g. in RStudio. From a plain shell
instead, wrap them as `Rscript -e '...'`.)

Every pull request is also validated by GitHub Actions across multiple
platforms and R versions (`R-CMD-check.yaml`), plus code coverage
(`coverage.yaml`) and the documentation site build (`pkgdown.yaml`).

the GPL-licensed dependencies (`RcppArmadillo`) it links against.

# Package index

## All functions

- [`allMetrics()`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/allMetrics.md)
  : Score an Estimated Graph Against a Ground-Truth DAG
- [`andesDAG`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/andesDAG.md)
  : Structure of the Andes Bayesian Network
- [`asiaDAG`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/asiaDAG.md)
  : Structure of the Asia Bayesian Network
- [`asiadf`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/asiadf.md)
  : Simulated Continuous Data from the Asia Network Structure
- [`cml()`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/cml.md) :
  CML Algorithm
- [`cml_mag()`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/cml_mag.md)
  : CML Algorithm (MAG-only output)
- [`plot_output()`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/plot_output.md)
  : Compare the Outputs from the Estimated and True Plots
- [`snl()`](https://stephenvsmith.github.io/lslearn/reference/snl.md) :
  SNL Algorithm
